title: Booting: from the BIOS to the first user program
subtitle: MS-DOS 4.00 and FreeBSD 15.1, from 0x7C00 to the first user process

slides.title: Real mode in one slide
bullets: Linear address = segment * 16 + offset, 20 bits, 1 MB
0000:7C00, 07C0:0000 and 0700:0C00 are the same byte
IVT at 0x0000, BIOS data area at 0x0400
BIOS services via INT 10h, 13h, 16h, 12h, 19h
Boot code reloads all segment registers and the stack
slides.notes: Every x86 CPU starts in real mode, the 8086's execution mode. Work two or three conversions on the board before showing any code. Stress that boot sectors set DS, ES and SS to zero so that offsets equal linear addresses.

slides.title: Numbers that shape every boot sector

stats.label: conventional memory, still the loader's limit

slides.notes: These four numbers appear in both code bases. The 640 KB limit is not only history: FreeBSD's loader Makefile still caps the loader at 500,000 bytes so that it fits below the video memory when booting through the BIOS.

slides.title: The first megabyte during boot
slides.caption: Linear addresses, not to scale. Both MBRs run at 0x600; FreeBSD fills 0x8C00-0xA000 with BTX and its client
slides.notes: All addresses are linear. The FreeBSD addresses come from .set lines in boot1.S and btx.S, the MS-DOS ones from EQUs in MSBOOT.ASM. The top of conventional memory is not a constant: both systems ask the BIOS.

slides.title: FDBOOT moves itself out of the way
slides.code:
sti             ;interrupts ok now
        cld
        mov di,0600h    ;where to relocate this boot record to
        mov cx,100h
        repnz movsw     ;relocate to 0:0600
;       jmp entry2
        db   0eah
        dw   $+4,0
entry2:
callouts: Copies 256 words from 0:7C00 to 0:0600
Far jump assembled by hand: EA, offset, segment
Frees 0x7C00 for the partition's boot sector
slides.notes: Every MBR must load the next sector to 0x7C00, where it is itself running, so it relocates first. Both MS-DOS and FreeBSD pick 0x600. The hand-assembled far jump is worth decoding with the class.

slides.title: What every MBR does
slides.caption: Relocate to 0x600, find the single active entry, load its first sector to 0x7C00, jump. boot0 replaces step 3 with a menu
slides.notes: Number the steps with the class. 1: the BIOS loads sector 0 to 0x7C00. 2: the MBR copies itself to 0x600 and far-jumps into the copy. 3: it scans the four entries at 0x1BE; none active means INT 18h, an invalid boot indicator or a second active entry means an error. 4: it reads the active partition's first sector to 0x7C00 and checks 55AA. 5: it jumps there with DL naming the drive and SI pointing at the entry. FDBOOT uses CHS and drive 0x80; mbr.S prefers EDD and trusts DL when valid.

slides.title: Three MBR programs

left.heading: MS-DOS 4.00 FDBOOT
bullets: Exactly one 0x80 entry, else 'Invalid partition table'
CHS reads only, five retries
Always reads BIOS drive 0x80
Never writes; FDISK keeps an existing MBR

right.heading: FreeBSD 15.1 mbr / boot0
bullets: mbr: same policy, same three messages
EDD packet reads when available, CHS fallback
boot0: F-key menu with timeout
boot0 writes the chosen default back to sector 0

slides.notes: mbr.S is the closest FreeBSD relative of FDBOOT; even its error strings match. boot0 adds a user interface in the same 512 bytes. boot0cfg(8) edits boot0's configuration bytes from user space.

slides.title: boot0 remembers your choice
slides.code:
shlb $0x4,%al                   # Point to
                addw $partbl,%ax                #  selected
                xchgw %bx,%ax                   #  partition
                movb $0x80,(%bx)                # Flag active
        /*
         * If not asked to do a write-back (flags 0x40) don't do one.
         * Around the call, save the partition pointer to %bx and
         * restore to %si which is where the next stage expects it.
         */
        1:      pushw %bx                       # Save
                testb $NOUPDATE,_FLAGS(%bp)     # No updates?
                jnz 2f                          # skip update
                movw $start,%bx                 # Data to write
                movb $0x3,%ah                   # Write sector
                callw intx13                    #  to disk
        2:      popw %si                        # Restore
callouts: The selected entry becomes active
Whole sector at 0x600 written to LBA 0
Skipped when NOUPDATE is set (timeout, noupdate)
slides.notes: The write happens before the selected boot sector is read and checked. Its return status is ignored. Study case 1.B contrasts this with gptboot's checksummed GPT update and with MS-DOS boot code, which never writes.

slides.title: When boot code writes to the disk
slides.caption: boot0 rewrites sector 0 only after a key press and unless NOUPDATE is set; MS-DOS boot code only reads
slides.notes: Trace both paths through boot0: a key press saves the option, marks the entry active and, unless flag 0x40 is set, writes the whole sector back before the chosen boot sector is even read. Timeout or Enter sets NOUPDATE, so nothing is written. Right: MS-DOS leaves all writing to FDISK, FORMAT and SYS; gptboot writes too, but to two checksummed GPT copies.

slides.title: MSBOOT's BIOS Parameter Block (selected fields)
slides.notes: The defaults describe a small hard disk; FORMAT overwrites them with the real medium's BPB and patches Phydrv. Offsets were checked against a sector assembled from this tree. Fields from 0x01C on are new in 4.00.

slides.title: MSBOOT checks the first two directory entries
slides.code:
MOV     DI,BX
        MOV     CX,11
        MOV     SI,OFFSET BIO           ; point to "ibmbio  com"
        REPZ    CMPSB                   ; see if the same
        JNZ     CKERR                   ; if not there advise the user
;
; Found the BIOS.  Check the second directory entry.
;
        LEA     DI,[BX+20h]
        MOV     SI,OFFSET DOS           ; point to "ibmdos  com"
        MOV     CX,11
        REPZ    CMPSB
        JZ      DoLoad
callouts: Directory sector was read to 0:0500
Names are IO.SYS and MSDOS.SYS in this build
Mismatch: 'Non-System disk or disk error'
slides.notes: The comments still mention IBMBIO and IBMDOS, but IBMCOPYRIGHT is FALSE in VERSION.INC, so this tree assembles the Microsoft names. Ask students where the names sit in the sector: offsets 0x1DB to 0x1F0.

slides.title: Constraints MSBOOT puts on a bootable disk
bullets: IO.SYS and MSDOS.SYS must be the first two directory entries
IO.SYS must start at the first data sector
Its first three sectors (MSLOAD) must be contiguous
Sector numbers must stay below SECLIM * 65536
No retries; 11 bytes of the sector left free
slides.notes: Each constraint maps to a few lines of code: the two REPZ CMPSB comparisons, the DoLoad loop, IBMLOADSIZE, and the overflow guard in DODIV. This is why SYS.COM exists. MSLOAD in IO.SYS lifts the contiguity limit for the rest of the file.

slides.title: Two boot chains
slides.caption: On GPT disks, pmbr replaces boot0 or mbr, and gptboot replaces boot1 and boot2
slides.notes: MS-DOS needs three small loaders and never leaves real mode. FreeBSD needs a protected-mode environment early because its loaders are C programs that read UFS, ELF and Lua. On GPT disks, pmbr and gptboot replace boot0/mbr and boot1/boot2.

slides.title: BTX calls the BIOS in real mode, not V86 mode
slides.code:
intusr.7:       movl %cr0,%eax                  # Leave
                dec %al                         #  protected
                movl %eax,%cr0                  #  mode
                ljmpw $0x0,$intusr.8
intusr.8:       xorw %ax,%ax                    # Reset %ds
                movw %ax,%ds                    #  and
                movw %ax,%ss                    #  %ss
                lidt ivtdesc                    # Set IVT
                popl %es                        # Restore
                popl %ds                        #  seg
                popl %fs                        #  regs
                popl %gs
                popal                           # Restore gp regs
                movw $MEM_ESPR-0x16,%sp         # Switch to real mode stack
                iret                            # Call target routine
callouts: Clears CR0.PE: back to real mode
Reloads the real-mode IVT
IRET into the BIOS routine; rret_tramp returns
slides.notes: The interface is still named v86, but nothing in the 15.1 btx.S sets PSL_VM. Clients such as boot2 fill a v86 structure and execute INT 31h; BTX switches modes around the BIOS call. Check older descriptions against the pinned source.

slides.title: One BIOS call from a BTX client
slides.caption: Client in ring 3, BTX in ring 0, the BIOS in real mode: every disk read makes this round trip
slides.notes: Follow boot2's drvread(): it fills struct v86 and __v86int executes INT 31h. BTX sets up rret_tramp as the return address, clears CR0.PE, reloads the real-mode IVT and IRETs into xread in the relocated boot1, which calls the BIOS. The return lands in rret_tramp, which re-enters protected mode and hands the registers back to the client.

slides.title: MSINIT finds MSDOS.SYS with MSBOOT's leftovers
callouts: Starting cluster of the second directory entry
The boot sector's buffer is part of the interface
slides.notes: MSINIT does not search the directory again; it reads the cluster number straight from the sector MSBOOT left at 0:0500. Then it follows the FAT chain and jumps to SYSINIT.

slides.title: SYSINIT starts the first user program
slides.code:
MOV     BX,OFFSET COMEXE        ; Point to EXEC block
        MOV     WORD PTR [BX.EXEC0_COM_LINE+2],CS       ; Set segments
        MOV     WORD PTR [BX.EXEC0_5C_FCB+2],CS
        MOV     WORD PTR [BX.EXEC0_6C_FCB+2],CS
        XOR     AX,AX                   ;Load and go
        MOV     AH,EXEC
        STC                             ;IN CASE OF INT 24
        INT     21H                     ;GO START UP COMMAND
        ENDIF
; NOTE FALL THROUGH IF EXEC RETURNS (an error)

COMERR:
        MOV     DX,OFFSET BADCOM        ;WANT TO PRINT COMMAND ERROR
        INVOKE  BADFIL
STALL:  JMP     STALL
callouts: INT 21h function 4Bh, AL=0: load and execute
Default program \COMMAND.COM /P, or SHELL=
If EXEC returns: error message, then STALL
slides.notes: By this point SYSINIT has moved itself to the top of memory, moved MSDOS.SYS into place, called DOSINIT, and processed CONFIG.SYS in several passes. The EXEC of the shell is where this module ends on the MS-DOS side.

slides.title: From the loader into 64-bit long mode
slides.code:
/* Now we're in compatibility mode. set %cs for long mode */
        movl    $VTOP(gdtdesc), %eax
        movl    VTOP(entry_hi), %esi
        movl    VTOP(entry_lo), %edi
        lgdt    (%eax)
        ljmp    $0x8, $VTOP(longmode)

        .code64
longmode:
        /* We're still running V=P, jump to entry point */
        movl    %esi, %eax
        salq    $32, %rax
        orq     %rdi, %rax
        pushq   %rax
        ret
callouts: Paging on, in compatibility mode
Far jump to a 64-bit code segment
Push the kernel entry, then ret
slides.notes: The Lua loader (loader.lua, config.lua) reads loader.conf and loads the kernel and modules; elf64_exec() then builds the module metadata and simple page tables and calls this trampoline through BTX's exec service. The kernel's btext receives modulep and kernend on the stack.

slides.title: mi_startup(): the whole kernel start-up loop
callouts: Always takes the first (lowest) entry
Entries added during boot are merged in order
Never returns: thread0 sleeps afterwards
slides.notes: Before this, locore.S btext passed modulep and kernend to hammer_time(), which parsed the loader metadata and set up the CPU. After hammer_time() returns a stack, mi_startup() runs every SYSINIT in sorted order.

slides.title: start_init(): becoming /sbin/init
callouts: Runs in process 1, created by create_init()
Tries each entry of init_path
EJUSTRETURN: return to user mode as init
slides.notes: create_init() forked process 1 at SI_SUB_CREATE_INIT; kick_init() made it runnable at SI_SUB_KTHREAD_INIT. start_init() mounts root, then execs /sbin/init. If nothing can be executed, the kernel panics with 'no init'.

slides.title: MS-DOS SYSINIT: CONFIG.SYS keywords
slides.code:
DB      7,"BUFFERS",  'B'
        DB      5,"BREAK",    'C'
        DB      6,"DEVICE",   'D'
        DB      5,"FILES",    'F'
        DB      4,"FCBS",     'X'
        DB      9,"LASTDRIVE",'L'
        db     10,"MULTITRACK", 'M'     ;AN002;
        DB      8,"DRIVPARM", 'P'       ; RS for DOS 3.2
                IF     STACKSW
        DB      6,"STACKS",   'K'       ; BAS for DOS 3.2
                ENDIF
        DB      7,"COUNTRY",  'Q'
        DB      5,"SHELL",    'S'
        db      7,"INSTALL",  'I'       ;AN000;
        db      3,"IFS",      'J'       ;AN000;
callouts: ORGANIZE turns each keyword into a letter
Unknown keywords become Z
INSTALL= lines run in a later pass
slides.notes: SYSINIT is a one-shot module that interprets a text file. Order of work is order of instructions plus fixed passes over the file. Third-party drivers join through DEVICE= and are linked at the head of the device chain.

slides.title: FreeBSD SYSINIT(): a declaration in a linker set
slides.code:
#define C_SYSINIT(uniquifier, subsystem, order, func, ident)    \
        static struct sysinit uniquifier ## _sys_init = {       \
                subsystem,                                      \
                order,                                          \
                { NULL },                                       \
                func,                                           \
                (ident)                                         \
        };                                                      \
        DATA_WSET(sysinit_set, uniquifier ## _sys_init)
#endif

#define SYSINIT(uniquifier, subsystem, order, func, ident)      \
        C_SYSINIT(uniquifier, subsystem, order,                 \
        (sysinit_cfunc_t)(sysinit_nfunc_t)func, (void *)(ident))
callouts: Static struct sysinit per use
Pointer placed in ELF section set_sysinit_set
Sorted by subsystem, then order
slides.notes: Any kernel file or module can declare work for any stage. The linker collects the pointers; mi_startup() sorts them. Preloaded modules' entries are merged into the same list; kldload'ed modules run their own entries at load time.

slides.title: Two SYSINITs side by side
slides.caption: MS-DOS: fixed passes over CONFIG.SYS, then EXEC of the shell. FreeBSD: a sorted linker set, then /sbin/init
slides.notes: Top: SYSINIT reads CONFIG.SYS, ORGANIZE turns keywords into letters, and the passes run in a fixed order, so every INSTALL= program runs after every DEVICE= driver. Bottom: no central list; SYSINIT() entries from any file or module land in set_sysinit_set, mi_startup() sorts them by (subsystem, order) and calls each, and two of them create and start process 1.

1.2 Trace MSBOOT into IO.SYS with QEMU and GDB

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Both systems start from the same 512-byte BIOS contract
MS-DOS: three tiny real-mode loaders, then SYSINIT and COMMAND.COM
FreeBSD: BTX, a C loader in protected mode, then long mode
Boot code that writes to disk trades safety for convenience
SYSINIT: a one-shot module versus a sorted declarative table
slides.notes: Ask students which design decisions follow from 1980s hardware and which are still visible today. Point out that FreeBSD's BIOS path still lives within the same 640 KB and 512-byte limits that shaped MS-DOS.
